title: quote mark inside URL that is attribute value is conflict
body:
Suppose I have an HTML element, it has an attribute, and its value is supposed to be a URL. The URL that I want to write includes pairs of straight double and single quotation marks, such as: http://example.com/file?q=super"wonder'truple'record"tennis

These characters as raw are legal for URLs under RFC 1738 section 2.2 because they're in US-ASCII (http://www.columbia.edu/kermit/ascii.html) as printable graphic characters and so they don't need to be percent-encoded but the double quotation mark is unsafe because it may be a delimiter in some systems (a function normally served elsewhere by angle brackets) while the apostrophe or single quotation mark is safe and may be percent-unencoded. This appears to me to be a bit ambivalent about the double quotation mark, especially if someone reads the RFC only as far as "URLs are written only with the graphic printable characters of the US-ASCII coded character set." and erroneously concludes that both of these marks may be in URLs (and, if they think that, then there's no bar to their using them multiple times within one URL).

RFC 3986 section 2.2, on URIs, thus including URLs, reserves the apostrophe and thus it must be percent-encoded; the same RFC, in appendix C, states that the double quotation mark is a delimiter along with angle brackets and the space. RFC 3986 is thus clearer for compliance than RFC 1738, but some systems may be relying on RFC 1738 since it more specifically applies to URLs.

Apparently, both double quote marks and apostrophes are being used unencoded in some URLs. That this problem has been found in the wild is suggested by an article telling people to stop using these characters in URLs (https://perishablepress.com/stop-using-unsafe-characters-in-urls/).

If a URL like this is kept in use because it works on someone's server and they're too busy to care about my or your complaint, and if it points to interesting content, we may want to cite it on a page of ours. We may need to put the URL into an HTML element attribute value requiring a URL. I might write <a href= . . . >.

HTML 5.2 section 4.8.2 (on the href attribute) thence section 2.5.1 (defining URL) requires that the URL conform to RFC 3986 or 3987 (the latter is on IRIs). The URL Living Standard at https://url.spec.whatwg.org/ is interesting and to be monitored but is not binding for HTML 5.2 compliance.

I routinely write double quotation marks around any HTML element attribute value. Where it's not required, I like it for style for consistency in authoring. It appears under HTML 5.2 that I don't have to surround the URL as a value with any quotation marks. But whether I delimit that way or not won't matter if a parser sees the characters within the URL and, in compliance with HTML 5.2, treats them as HTML delimiters and truncates the URL, giving an unpredictable result.

I don't think I can percent-encode the URL as the attribute's value and expect the user agent (usually a browser) to percent-decode it. Besides, I probably won't notice that a long URL has one of these characters and thus needs percent-encoding.

(URLs and RFCs are as accessed Apr. 22, 2020.)

Is there a solution to this?

One solution I imagine would be to add an attribute on whether to parse the href value as percent-encoded by the HTML author, with the new attribute being true/false. The absence of the attribute would be treated as if it is present with a value of false (i.e., don't percent-decode). If the value is explicitly true, the HTML author would then percent-encode any questionable character in the URL and parsers would percent-decode the URL. Setting the value to true and then failing to percent-encode the URL when percent-encoding is needed would likely result in an error due to percent-decoding producing a URL different from the original URL.

I doubt this is being implemented in the wild now, but I don't know of any solution that is being implemented now, and it appears that the problem is in the wild, so it appears that a solution has to be proposed.
